newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Hutu refugees die in Zaire, no date yet for talks.
newsitem.headline: Hutu refugees die in Zaire, no date yet for talks.

text.p: Rwandan Hutu refugees stranded around a railway line in Zaire's war zone are dropping and dying for lack of food, water and medicine while unburied bodies lie in the remote rain forest, aid agencies say.

The U.N. refugee agency UNHCR said on Saturday it was trying to negotiate an emergency relief plan with Laurent Kabila's rebels and devising ways to repatriate the Hutus -- many of whom have been begging to return home.

It said the rebels had blocked an attempt to deliver aid to 20,000 refugees in a make-shift camp at Lula outside Zaire's rebel-held third city of Kisangani but that a second train-load of aid left on Saturday for two points south of Lula.
"Without the crucial elements (of this plan) the people will start dying in very large numbers. Many have already died," Filippo Grandi, the agency's representative in Goma, said.
"There is a risk of serious epidemics if we don't bring water very quickly," he told Reuters.
Tens of thousands of refugees are stranded along a railway line south of Kisangani, which rebels captured on March 15.
UNHCR regional spokesman Paul Stromberg said by telephone from Kisangani that the rebels wanted the refugees to move further south before receiving aid.
"They are completely exhausted. They are dying like flies," said Marcel van Soest, head of Doctors Without Borders (MSF) in Goma.
The Zairean Red Cross says 500 people have been buried and bodies litter the surrounding countryside.
On the battle front, Zaire's army chief of staff, General Mahele Lieko Bokoungo, said his forces still held the Shaba town of Kasenga -- dismissing reports that it had fallen to rebels.
A defence ministry official said the army had attacked rebels holding the town of Moba on Lake Tanganyika after approaching by boat.
A spokesman for Kabila's rebels said negotiations with envoys of ailing president Mobutu Sese Seko would start early next week probably in South Africa but there was no confirmation of any firm date.
The U.N. World Food Programme, UNHCR and the Zairean Red Cross sent the first train-load of 120 tonnes of food and medicine to the refugees on Thursday and Friday.

Emaciated refugees, some almost skeletal, awaited the train. Some were trying to walk to Kisangani while those too weak to start the trek lay dead and dying within an abandoned camp at Ubilo, a village 82 km (51 miles) south of Kisangani.
"If they can get through to Kisangani there may be some hope but if they have to go back to Ubundu (125 km, 78 miles south of Kisangani) then half of them could die," MSF's van Soest said.

More than a million Hutus fled camps on the Rwandan and Burundian border last October and November after the rebels took up arms in the area vowing to topple Mobutu, who has dominated Zaire since a 1965 military coup.

Around 600,000 returned to Rwanda in November via Goma but hundreds of thousands more fled west into the jungle with former Rwandan government soldiers and militias held responsible for massacres during Rwanda's 1994 genocide of minority Tutsis.
Since then the refugees have set up a series of makeshift camps and fled before advancing rebels, many of them Tutsis, in a trek that has hampered relief efforts.
